properties.name: Lucali
properties.blurb: A converted candy store turned into one of the city's most sought-after coal-oven pies. No slices, cash only, and a line that starts before opening — reserve ahead or plan to wait.

properties.name: Di Fara Pizza
properties.blurb: The benchmark by which a lot of NYC pizza gets judged. Founder Dom DeMarco built the reputation over decades; the family runs it today with the same hand-snipped basil finish.

properties.name: L'Industrie Pizzeria
properties.blurb: A Williamsburg slice shop built around one standout order: a fior di latte square topped with cold burrata and basil after it comes out of the oven. Expect a line most evenings — it's become one of the most talked-about slices in the city since opening in 2015.

properties.name: Roberta's
properties.blurb: The wood-fired pizzeria that helped put Bushwick on the food map in 2008. Char-heavy, ingredient-driven pies in a graffitied warehouse space with a backyard garden — go for the Bee Sting, with soppressata, chili, and honey.

properties.name: Grimaldi's
properties.blurb: A DUMBO fixture since 1990, cooking coal-oven pies with a thin, blistered crust in the shadow of the Brooklyn Bridge. One of the pizzerias most credited with starting the modern NYC pizza pilgrimage.

properties.name: Juliana's
properties.blurb: Opened in 2012 by Patsy Grimaldi — the same Patsy behind the pizzeria next door that still carries his old name — in the very space where he first started. Same coal oven, same thin, char-edged crust; regulars debate endlessly which one is better.

properties.name: Totonno's
properties.blurb: Open since 1924 in Coney Island, one of the oldest coal-oven pizzerias in the country. Cash only, whole pies only, and still run by the founder's descendants — come for a slice of pizza history as much as the pizza.

properties.name: L&B Spumoni Gardens
properties.blurb: A Gravesend institution since the late 1930s, known for its upside-down square slices — sauce on top, cheese on the bottom — and the spumoni ice cream that gives the place its name.

properties.name: F & F Pizzeria
properties.blurb: A Carroll Gardens square-slice spot with a loyal local following and a reputation built on consistency more than spectacle — reliable, well-charred Sicilian squares from a no-frills counter.

properties.name: Best Pizza
properties.blurb: A Williamsburg spot best known for its grandma slice — crushed tomato, garlic, and a hit of chopped anchovy under a well-browned, lacy-crisp bottom crust. Also does a strong classic NY slice.

properties.name: Williamsburg Pizza
properties.blurb: A neighborhood mini-chain that built its name on grandma squares — thick, cheesy slices with a browned, oily crust — alongside a full rotation of classic and specialty pies.

properties.name: Layla Jones
properties.blurb: A Cobble Hill storefront serving an unusual pair of formats: a square 'Brooklyn Classic' with a bubbly crust, and a charcoal-grilled version with a thin, lightly charred, chewy crust closer to a bar pie.

properties.name: Paulie Gee's Slice Shop
properties.blurb: The casual counterpart to the original Paulie Gee's restaurant around the corner, which closed and reopened as a bar called Me and Paul's in 2026. Simple, old-school New York slices, including a solid Sicilian square, from the same team.

properties.name: Joe's Pizza
properties.blurb: The Greenwich Village original, open since 1975. No frills, fold-and-go, and about as close to a citywide consensus pick for classic NY slice as exists.

properties.name: Prince Street Pizza
properties.blurb: The spicy spring pepperoni square, curled and crisped at the edges, is the reason for the perpetual Nolita line. Get there off-peak if you don't want to wait.

properties.name: Rizzo's Fine Pizza
properties.blurb: An Astoria square-slice institution since the 1950s — thick, cheese-forward, and sauced on top in the old-school style. A neighborhood staple that draws people from across the borough.
